finance_aml.gbm.baseline_gap_note: This reaches minority-class F1 well below the published 0.6323 (GFP+XGBoost, AMLworld HI-Small, NeurIPS 2023 D&B). The cause is a feature ARCHITECTURE difference, not a tuning one: the gap is unreachable at any threshold, because measured AUPRC is far below what that F1 requires. IBM's Graph Feature Preprocessor computes per-transaction subgraph patterns over a dynamically updated graph; this project computes per-account scalar aggregates. A degree is one number per account, whereas a GFP feature is a pattern match in that transaction's own neighbourhood at the moment it arrives. GFP ships in `snapml` under a Proprietary licence and is excluded by this project's commercial-OK-only rule, but the licence is not itself the cause - the architecture is, and it is reimplementable without `snapml`, simply at more cost than renaming aggregates. Reachability is computed to 4 hops against injected CYCLE attempts of up to 10; that was previously recorded as a main cause and is NOT one - the GFP paper (arXiv:2402.08593) decomposes its own contribution, and its Table 5 (HI-Small, XGBoost, batch 128) gives fan-in/fan-out, which is reimplemented here, 37 F1 points (19.75 to 56.88) and multi-hop cycle and scatter-gather patterns 1.7 more (to 58.60; 'up to 4%' in its text is F1 points, not a relative gain). The evaluation is strictly inductive and temporally split. Per-account aggregates are causal (each row sees only edges strictly before it); the structural block - cycle closure, scatter-gather, bank diversity, burst degree - is still fitted on the training window, because recomputing sparse reachability at every timestep is not tractable here. Reported as measured; not adjusted to close the gap. Full workings: references/finance-gap-investigation.md.

calibration.does_not_move_ranking: Platt is STRICTLY monotone, so AUC and AUC-PR are unchanged by construction: measured Round 49, both are identical to the uncalibrated values to ten decimals, and that held for the map fitted on the probability and for the logit(s) map that now ships alike. The qualifier matters and was missing - isotonic is only WEAKLY monotone, and on this same split it moved AUROC by -0.00031674 and AUPRC by -0.01121590 (-9.09%). Calibration by a strictly monotone map fixes what a probability MEANS, never how the rows are ordered. ONE HONEST QUALIFIER ON THE MAP THAT SHIPS: logit() clips at 1e-12, so scores below 1e-12 or above 1-1e-12 would tie. None exist on this split (the raw range is 4.4e-11 to 0.99997), so no pair is tied and the AUCs above are exact; a retrain that saturates a leaf would need this re-checked rather than assumed.
calibration.fitted_on: validation split; scored on the held-out test split
calibration.formula: p = 1 / (1 + exp(a * logit(clip(score, logit_clip_eps, 1 - logit_clip_eps)) + b)), logit(q) = log(q / (1 - q))
calibration.reliability_diagram_defensible_here: YES on the test split, which carries 2,321 events. Van Calster et al. (J Clin Epidemiol 2016) ask for at least 200 events and 200 non-events before a flexible calibration curve, and Riley et al. (Stat Med 2021) show that such rules of thumb can still be too few. NO on the browser's evaluation sample: 8,192 rows from the same test window at a 0.02 base rate, so 164 events, which is why the page draws no curve and says so. Each number is right for its own denominator, and confusing the two is the mistake this repository documents under 'ask what the metric was divided by'. The floor also binds on medical (42 events) and satellite (113). The CORP terms below are reported regardless, because PAV picks no bin count and so they are stable where a binned curve is not.
calibration.why_not_isotonic: MEASURED Round 49 on this split, not argued: isotonic Brier 0.00142218 / log-loss 0.00820025 against 0.00142199 / 0.00818964 for the same fit_platt fed logit(s) - within noise on both proper scoring rules, so ICML 2005's 'as good as, or better than' holds here in the 'as good as' form. Platt is kept on the tie-break: isotonic is only WEAKLY monotone, collapsed 1,388,669 distinct scores to 138, and cost AUROC 0.00031674 and AUPRC 0.01121590 (-9.09%), while both Platt arms moved neither to ten decimals; it also emitted exactly 0 on 464,176 test rows, one a true positive, and 138 breakpoints are not two floats a browser can apply. ONE CORRECTION TO THE OLD REASONING SURVIVES HERE: the calibration set carries 801 events, not 2,321 (that is the test split). The second - that a/b were fitted on a PROBABILITY rather than a log-odds, making the map return 0.00090148 for nine of ten deciles - is FIXED, not outstanding: on_logit is true above and the map published here is the logit(s) arm those numbers describe. Workings: references/finance-calibration-isotonic-vs-platt.md.

finance_aml.scorecard.metric_note: Fitted by maximising net benefit across five decision thresholds rather than a surrogate loss. `fit_method` is 'coordinate-search': the objective it maximises is the exact AUNBC, but optimality is NOT claimed - the exact integer program over all (sample x threshold) indicators is not tractable at this row count, and reporting a heuristic's result as an optimum would be a different claim. `exact_under_bfv` records that the encrypted score equals the plaintext score bit for bit, which is the property a CKKS student cannot offer; verified in tests/test_scorecard_bfv_exact.py.

not_measured.published_source: PGS Catalog PPM001647 for PGS000004 (PRS313): AUROC 0.633 (95% CI 0.624-0.641), n=400,812 Europeans - 4,340 cases and 396,472 controls - from Jia et al., JNCI Cancer Spectrum 2020 (doi:10.1093/jncics/pkaa021). Verified at the Catalog REST record 2026-08-11. TWO CAVEATS THAT MAKE THIS A CITATION AND NOT A TARGET, both from the record itself: the model is fitted WITH COVARIATES - 'family history of cancer (in first-degree relatives), genotyping array' - which a bare weighted dot product does not have; and the cohort was 'missing 25 variants (8%) based on availability of variants in the cohort', so the published figure is for 288 of the 313 variants, not all of them. This replaced PGS000001's C-index 0.628 (PPM017270) when the score changed. That figure was a Harrell's C-index over censored follow-up, not an AUROC, and the two are not directly comparable - a C-index is computed over time-to-event pairs and an AUROC over a fixed case/control split. PGS000004 publishes a genuine AUROC, so the switch also removes that comparability problem rather than only changing the number.
not_measured.reason: 1000 Genomes is a reference panel with no breast-cancer case/control status. AUROC requires a phenotyped cohort, so the published figure is carried as a citation, not as a measurement from this run: 0.633 (AUROC (European ancestry)).

medical_fl.student.baseline_gap_note: This scores far below the 0.901 ResNet-18 baseline. The reason is representational rather than cryptographic: 3,226 parameters over a 14x14 input is a REPRESENTATION choice, not a feasibility limit - and this note said 'a CKKS-feasibility budget' until Round 32, which overstated how forced it was. Kim et al. (arXiv:2506.15258) do HE chest-X-ray inference on a VQGAN latent at downsampling factor 8 rather than on pixels, so the alternative to downsampling 28->14 is re-representing the input. The browser already runs onnxruntime-web, so such an encoder would run locally in plaintext with no privacy loss. Recorded as the sixth falsifiable trigger in the additional-model decision in docs/deliverable-verification.md, not acted on - and note that f=8 on a 28x28 input gives 3.5x3.5, so the transfer is the open measurement rather than a citation. This sentence claimed the trigger existed for two rounds while the table held five rows and none of them was this one; the trigger was written, and the decision moved to a tracked file so the claim can be checked. Round 24 found it had been WORSE than that - a constant predictor, emitting one class for all 156 test images, with accuracy 0.730769 exactly equal to the majority-class rate and AUC 0.354, below random. It was invisible because the registry declared `auc` while the record stored `accuracy`, and because this student had neither protection its teacher already had: class-weighted loss and AUC-based model selection. Both were added. Read `n_classes_predicted` and `majority_class_rate` beside the score - an accuracy equal to the majority rate is the signature of a model that learned nothing. Workings: references/medical-student-collapse-investigation.md.
medical_fl.student.metric_note: Two metrics are recorded and they answer different questions. `auc` is the registry's declared headline and is what the published baseline compares against. `student_metric`/`teacher_metric` are accuracy, because fidelity compares DECISIONS and a decision has no score to rank - so agreement and metric_delta are necessarily computed on a decision metric. Do not read the accuracy against the AUC baseline.

satellite_comms.telemanom.baseline_gap_note: Read n_events_scored before comparing this to the baseline. The scored test window holds 3 labelled anomaly event(s), not the 320 that n_anomaly_intervals counts over the whole timeline - the annotated anomalies sit earlier in the mission, so a temporal split leaves almost nothing to score. This run decomposes as tp=0 fp=2 fn=3, and the detector flags 2 of 441,600 points. The figure does not reproduce across identical-config retrains: two earlier runs recorded 0.714286 (tp=1 fp=0 fn=2) and 0.454545 (tp=1 fp=1 fn=2), one false-alarm run apart, both with the whole-series z-score this script used until Round 34. Three protocol gaps to the citation remain open and are stated rather than closed: ESA-ADB multiplies event precision by the time-level TNR (recorded here as corrected_event_wise_f0_5), it splits each mission in half where this tests on the last 30 percent, and its lightweight test partition holds 65 events against 3 here. Workings: references/satellite-event-count-investigation.md.
satellite_comms.telemanom.dataset: ESA Anomaly Dataset (ESA-ADB), Mission1 lightweight channels 41-46
satellite_comms.telemanom.metric_note: Event-wise F-beta at beta=0.5 under the overlap rule, which is what ESA-ADB and Telemanom report. Telemanom's widely-quoted 0.71 is F0.5, not F1. point_adjusted_f1 is shown only to expose how much point adjustment inflates: Kim et al. (AAAI 2022) show that under point adjustment even a random anomaly score can reach state-of-the-art. Only labels whose ESA-ADB Category is 'Anomaly' count as positives; the 690 annotated rare *nominal* events do not.
satellite_comms.telemanom.sample_size_note: Read n_events_scored before comparing this to published_lightweight_f0_5. The denominator of an event-wise metric is EVENTS, and a temporal split of this corpus leaves very few of them in the scored window: 320 labelled intervals over the whole timeline reduce to 3 inside the test window, because the annotated anomalies are concentrated earlier in the mission. The recorded score is therefore a small-sample figure and one event either way moves it by tenths - it is NOT comparable to a published benchmark computed over the full annotated set, however similar the two decimals look. The number is reported as measured rather than reweighted, and the sample size is reported beside it so the comparison is not made silently.

telecom_ids.nidd.baseline_gap_note: There is no baseline number to have a gap to, and that is a deliberate registry decision rather than a missing measurement: the two figures usually quoted for this corpus (99.61% for a classical CNN, 99.71% for a hybrid quantum-classical Quan-ConvCNN, Wang/Fok/Thing) are ACCURACIES on the BINARY benign-versus-malicious task, and this model is judged on 9-class macro F1, so putting them in `baseline` would render an accuracy beside a macro F1 as though the two were the same scale. WHAT THE COMPARISON CAN AND CANNOT SAY. This model scores about 0.9829 9-class accuracy with every row identifier and every host fingerprint dropped. Set beside binary accuracies, the 1.3-point difference is not a gap on one task. The 9-class anchors are the dataset paper's random forest at 99.48% accuracy on its top-10 features (Samarakoon et al., arXiv:2212.01298) and BiTAD (Future Internet 17(11) 482) at 0.9047; this model sits between them, on its own stratified random split rather than a shared one, so each is an anchor and not a head-to-head. WHAT THE COUNTERFACTUAL SHOWS. Restoring the corpus's integer row counters takes accuracy to about 0.9997, recorded every run as `leak_counterfactual_accuracy`: that is what a row counter is worth on this corpus. It does not show what the published figures used, because 0.9829 is reachable here with no identifiers at all, using one additional flow statistic (`IdleTime`) that Combined.csv does not carry. Whether the published figures lean on identifiers is OPEN: the dataset paper's top-10 inputs include the sequence number `Seq` and `Offset`, Wang/Fok/Thing's inputs include `Offset`, both columns are dropped here, and no published ablation settles it.

telecom_ids.nidd.framing: Real 5G network traffic, 9 attack classes, 47 flow-statistic features. This is a NETWORK-LAYER model and a different task from the QKD-layer classifier on the same page - no shared labels, no shared features, so the two scores are not a comparison. IT IS FITTED ON THE FIELDS-PRESERVED EXPORT (113 columns) AND WAS FITTED ON Combined.csv (52) UNTIL ROUND 50, which is the single most important thing to know about the numbers here: the same rows and the same classes, but the narrow export omits `IdleTime` and that one column is worth 22 points of accuracy. `idle_time_ablation` re-measures this every run by refitting without it, and the result reproduces what this model used to score. Two controls are recorded beside the headline and both are worth more than the headline. `idle_time_ablation` says the old weakness was a choice of export, not a property of the corpus. `leak_counterfactual_accuracy` says that restoring four integer row counters takes accuracy to about 0.9997, which is not a better model but a leak.

idle_time_ablation.what_this_means: Removing `IdleTime` ALONE costs essentially the same accuracy as removing all six columns Combined.csv omits, and both land on the score this model published while it was fitted on Combined.csv. The other five - `Dir`, `Flgs`, `TcpOpt`, `sVlan`, `dVlan` - are worth 0.0006 accuracy between them. So the model's former weakness was one absent flow statistic, not the corpus and not the method. THAT IS REDUNDANCY AND NOT EMPTINESS, stated because the shorter version would be false. Two of those five are individually strong - `Dir` scores one-vs-rest AUC 0.9811 on ICMPFlood and `TcpOpt` 0.9433 on SlowrateDoS, both above the 0.90 threshold `single_feature_leak_check` uses, and both appear in its flagged list. What the ablation shows is that the other 41 columns already carry what they carry. `IdleTime` IS NOT AN IDENTIFIER and the distinction is the same one `leak_counterfactual_*` exists to draw: it takes 17 distinct integer values over 1,215,890 rows, so it cannot encode a row position, and it separates `SlowrateDoS` - an attack defined by holding a connection idle - at one-vs-rest AUC 0.9574. A row counter that scores that well describes where a row sits in a file. This describes what the traffic did.

linear_baseline.what_it_is: multinomial logistic regression on the 37 NUMERIC features only, standardised, fitted directly rather than distilled. The 10 ordinal codes are excluded because their integer order is nominal and a linear model would read it as a magnitude. Recorded as the classical floor and as a feasibility probe for a future CKKS-linear tier: it predicts 9 of 9 classes, so a linear student on this corpus does not collapse the way an 8-class one nearly does elsewhere in this project.

telecom_ids.nidd.metric_note: THE TWO NUMBERS STILL READ THE OPPOSITE WAY ROUND FROM EVERY OTHER MODEL IN THIS PROJECT, and the refit onto the wide export did NOT fix that - it shrank it. Everywhere else here the aggregate flatters and the per-class figure exposes it, which is why `aggregate_accuracy` is rendered as the companion 'shown so the gap is visible'. On this corpus macro F1 is still the OPTIMISTIC number and aggregate accuracy still the PESSIMISTIC one. What changed is the size of the disagreement: macro F1 minus accuracy was 0.1655 on the narrow export (0.9263 against 0.7608) and is about 0.0121 now (0.9950 against 0.9829). THE MECHANISM IS UNCHANGED, which is the part a reader is most likely to get wrong. It is not that a small class now drags the macro average - the smallest class, ICMPFlood at 289 test rows, scores 1.0000 and lifts it. It is the same two majority classes as before: Benign at 39.3% of rows and UDPFlood at 37.6% are the only pair that confuses at all, they carry 77% of the test set between them, so accuracy is dominated by them while a macro average over 9 classes is carried by the seven scoring 0.9999 or better. Adding `IdleTime` separated that pair almost completely rather than changing which pair it is. The residual is one directional confusion - UDPFlood predicted as Benign - and it is 1.71% of the test set against 23.92% before. Read `per_class_f1` and it is visible directly: the two lowest entries are Benign and UDPFlood, and every other class is at or above 0.9999. Neither figure is the flattering one to quote alone.
telecom_ids.nidd.sample_size_note: Trained and scored on the whole of 5G-NIDD BTS1_BTS2_fields_preserved.csv - 1,215,890 flows, stratified 75/25 at seed 42, so the test split is 303,973 rows and every class keeps its corpus proportion. Row for row this is the same corpus as Combined.csv, which this model used until Round 50; only the column count differs, 113 against 52. No subsampling and no class rebalancing: `ICMPFlood` is 1,155 rows in the corpus and 289 in the test split, which is small but is the real prevalence, and resampling it would report a per-class F1 for a distribution the deployed model never sees. The browser evaluation sample is a different matter and is NOT proportional - see the note in eval_sample.json, which states its per-class floor and why its macro F1 is not this one.

single_feature_leak_check.what_this_means: One-vs-rest rank-AUC per feature per class, at the 0.90 threshold scripts/prep_model_inputs.py already publishes against, measured AFTER all 66 drops. A LARGE NUMBER HERE IS EXPECTED ON THIS CORPUS AND IS NOT THE LEAK THIS MODEL IS ABOUT. The attacks are generated by distinct tools against distinct services, so a scan, a SYN flood and a slow-rate HTTP attack genuinely differ in TTL, packet rate, TCP window and ACK timing - these are the flow statistics an intrusion detector is supposed to use. The check's own docstring anticipates the case and warns rather than failing. The distinction that matters is against `leak_counterfactual_*`: `Unnamed: 0`, `Rank`, `Seq` and `Offset` cleared the same threshold while being bookkeeping columns that carry no information about the traffic at all, which is why those four are dropped and these are kept. `IdleTime` is in this list and is the case that shows the rule is not circular - it clears the threshold on SlowrateDoS, it is the single most valuable column in the corpus by `idle_time_ablation`, and it takes 17 distinct integer values over 1.2 million rows, so no amount of it can address a row. Recorded rather than described so the distinction is checkable.

telecom_ids.qml.classical_rf_attribution_note: Impurity importance (training split, biased toward high-cardinality features) and permutation importance (held-out split, scored on macro F1, 20 repeats, std reported). Read the permutation figure where they disagree. These rank which features of a SYNTHETIC corpus this forest needs, not signals from a real QKD link. Two planted features are nearly redundant: sift_ratio separates detector_blinding perfectly on its own yet costs almost nothing to remove, because click_asymmetry separates the same class; and dark_count_rate is within one std of zero. Exact linear SHAP does not apply to a tree ensemble, which is why these two measures are used instead.
telecom_ids.qml.data: synthetic, class structure per arXiv:2509.14282 (Al-Kuwari et al., 2025)

export.int8_skipped_reason: tree ensemble: parameters live in node attributes, not weight tensors, so dynamic int8 quantisation has nothing to quantise

telecom_ids.qml.framing: Architecture comparison, not a performance claim. The published model is the random forest; the quantum-kernel SVC and the variational QNN are recorded beside it and not published. The data is synthetic because no commercial-OK real QKD-attack corpus exists. Published QML-IDS results are mixed rather than uniformly below a random forest: Al-Kuwari et al. (arXiv:2509.14282) report a hybrid QLSTM at 94.7% against their own random forest, while arXiv:2512.05069 was withdrawn by its own authors for insufficient evaluation. Per-class F1 is the headline; aggregate accuracy is shown beside it because Engelen et al. (WTMC 2021) demonstrated it stays at 0.99 across a label correction that moved Bot F1 from 0.60 to 0.99.

telecom_ids.student.argmax_location: client, in plaintext, after decrypting all 8 class scores
telecom_ids.student.metric_note: Read `n_classes_predicted` before `macro_f1`. A linear student that stops predicting a class scores 0 on it by construction, and macro F1 then averages in a zero that looks like poor discrimination rather than an absent output - this repo's own QNN carries exactly that defect and is documented as doing so, so the check is not hypothetical. `agreement` is recorded but is NOT evidence the minority classes survived: agreement on the finance student rose from 0.884 to 0.947 across a change that left minority-class F1 unmoved, which is why per-class F1 is the headline here and the aggregate is a companion.
